Gloria Mundi.

where they ought to have taken <term>pyrites</term>, <gloss>a metallic sulfide</gloss>, <term>sulphur</term>, <term>salt</term>, <term>metal</term>, and diverse other materials, they took instead substances in which there is no operation. These things are considered precious in the shops, yet they have absolutely no value in this labor. Truly, our matter is not bought from any shop, yet it is found there every day, and merchants throw it into the streets. It is enough, therefore, that it is found for free. But the matter of our <term>stone</term> is compared to all those things with which the craftsmen labor: for our stone is our <term>salt</term>, our <term>mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term>, <term>nitre</term>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulphur</term>, and infinite others of that kind, not dug from wild or rustic mountains with hammers and other instruments. Our stone is unearthed solely from our own mountains and fountains: in our <term>salt-fountain</term> is our <term>salt</term> found; from our earth is our metal, <term>mercury</term>, and <term>sulphur</term> cast, and not from wild, foreign, or rustic mountains, all of which the craftsmen do not understand, nor can they believe or comprehend. For the Lord has darkened and closed their senses, for which reason they used these things otherwise than they ought to have been used, and they did not aim at the target in the slightest. Nevertheless, they persisted in this contrary direction and followed their own stubborn heads; for when they ought to have <term>distilled</term> gently, they <term>sublimed</term> <gloss>vaporized and condensed</gloss> with a strong fire, they scorched their <term>strong waters</term> <gloss>acids</gloss>, and immediately burned the operation of nature and the things themselves, reducing them to nothing. Even when they should have <term>solved</term> <gloss>dissolved</gloss>, they <term>coagulated</term> <gloss>solidified</gloss> instead, and again, like those unskilled in things, they handled the matter ineptly and fell into doubt, claiming with lying words that the art is not true but false. In this, however, they rightly lie, for their own ignorance shamefully deceived them, which must be imputed to their own dark and murky cunning, while, according to their obscure intellect, they interpreted words otherwise than they sounded. For example, when the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> (which they call grinding), those unskilled <term>philosophasters</term> <gloss>pseudo-philosophers</gloss> understood it as burning, and reduced the things entirely to ashes, such that nothing could be made from them. <summary>This page warns against the mistakes of unskilled practitioners who misinterpret alchemical terminology, emphasizing that the true materials are common and simple rather than rare shop-bought substances.</summary>
